q.intro.text: A high school surveyed its two hundred juniors: does each one have a part-time job, and a driver’s license? The counselor picks one of the juniors with a job at random. What is the probability that this junior has a license? Pick one, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps on the same table. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the notation.

e.step0.text: Each inside cell is an and: forty-eight juniors have a job and a license. The margins are single groups: eighty have a job, a hundred and ten have a license, two hundred in all.

e.step1.text: Given a job rules out everyone in the no job row. Only the job row is left: its total, eighty, is the new whole. That is what the bar in P of L given J means.

e.step2.text: Inside the new whole, forty-eight have a license: P of L given J is forty-eight over eighty, which is three fifths. Three out of every five juniors with a job can drive.

e.step3.text: With probabilities it is the same move: P of L given J equals P of L and J, divided by P of J. That is forty-eight over two hundred, divided by eighty over two hundred. The two hundreds cancel, and forty-eight over eighty is left. Dividing by P of J is making the job row the whole.

e.why.text: Quick check: why divide by eighty and not by two hundred?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. The junior was picked from those with a job, so nobody else is possible: the eighty are the whole.

e.why.all.text: The two hundred include a hundred and twenty juniors with no job, and none of them can be picked. The condition shrinks the whole.

e.why.inv.text: The hundred and ten are the juniors with a license. Dividing by them answers the reverse question: of the license holders, how many have a job?

t.intro.text: A music teacher surveys a hundred and sixty students: left or right handed, and do they play an instrument? Is playing an instrument independent of being left handed? The first step is done for you.

t.cond.text: Of the left handed students, what fraction play an instrument? That is P of I given L.

t.cond.ok.text: Yes: six of the sixteen left handers, six sixteenths, which is three eighths.

t.cond.all.text: Six over a hundred and sixty divides by every student. Given left handed, only the sixteen left handers count.

t.cond.inv.text: Six over sixty looks inside the instrument players: that is P of L given I. The condition here is left handed.

t.cond.no.text: The left handed row is the whole: sixteen students. How many of them play?

t.all.text: Now with no condition: of all one hundred and sixty students, what fraction play an instrument? That is P of I.

t.all.ok.text: Yes: sixty of a hundred and sixty, which is three eighths.

t.all.left.text: Sixteen over a hundred and sixty is the share who are left handed. Count all the players: the plays column total.

t.all.joint.text: Six over a hundred and sixty is only the left handed players. All players: the column total, sixty.

t.all.no.text: Use the plays column total over the grand total.

t.judge.text: P of I given L is three eighths, and P of I is three eighths. So are the two events independent?

t.judge.ok.text: Right: knowing a student is left handed does not change the chance they play. The events are independent.

t.judge.cell.text: Only six sounds small, but there are only sixteen left handers. Compare shares, not one cell: three eighths and three eighths.

t.judge.story.text: How it sounds does not decide it. The shares are equal, so the condition changes nothing.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked forty-eight over eighty, and you were right: the juniors with a job are the whole.

q.cb.all.text: At the start you picked forty-eight over two hundred. That divides by every junior. Given a job, only the eighty with a job count: forty-eight over eighty.

q.cb.inv.text: At the start you picked forty-eight over a hundred and ten. That is the share of license holders who have a job: the reverse question. Here it is forty-eight over eighty.

q.cb.none.text: Conditioning shrinks the whole to the condition’s row or column, then you count inside it.

p.intro.text: Roll one die. A: the roll is one or two. B: the roll is six. A and B can never happen together. Sam says: mutually exclusive events have nothing to do with each other, so they are independent. Is Sam right?

p.test.text: Let’s test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. No face is in both circles: the overlap is empty.

p.c2.text: Right. One third times one sixth is one eighteenth, more than zero.

p.c3.text: Right. And look: given B, A is impossible. P of A given B is zero, but P of A is one third.

p.no.disj.text: Having no outcomes in common is the strongest link there is: if B happens, A can’t.

p.no.example.text: One die example doesn’t prove a rule. The reason has to work for every pair of events.

p.no.unequal.text: Different probabilities don’t decide anything: independent events can have different probabilities too.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That’s a proof, and it works for any mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities: P of A and B is zero, but P of A times P of B is more than zero. They are dependent. The one exception is an impossible event, with probability zero.
